title: Repeat until done
hook: Make Python repeat steps for you, then stop at the right moment.

warmup.q: `score = 75`. Which line shows? `if score >= 90: A` / `elif score >= 70: B` / `else: C`
warmup.explain: 75 is not 90 or more, so the first road is skipped. It is 70 or more, so B runs and the rest is skipped.

warmup.q: You type 5 when `n = input("Number? ")` asks. What is `n`?
warmup.explain: input() always gives text. Use int(n) when you need a real number.
Two things: the colon at the end, and the comparison is written >= not =>.

why.heading: Computers love boring repeats
why.text: A slate shows take 1, take 2, take 3, take 4. You could write four print lines. But 400? A **loop** repeats lines for you, as many times as you need. Write the steps once, let Python do them again and again.

why.heading: while: repeat while it is true
why.text:
`while` looks like `if`:

`while take <= 3:`
`    print(take)`

But after running the pushed-in lines, Python jumps back up and asks the question again. As long as it is True, round it goes. When it turns False, Python moves on below.

why.heading: The counter
why.text: A loop needs something that changes, or it never ends. Usually a **counter**: `take = 1` before the loop, and `take += 1` inside it. `+= 1` means add 1 to take. It is short for `take = take + 1`.

why.heading: break: leave right now
why.text:
Sometimes you want out in the middle. `break` jumps out of the loop at once. `while True:` means keep going forever, because True is always True. You leave with `break`, usually inside an if:

`if name == "done":`
`    break`

why.heading: The infinite loop mistake
why.text: If the question never turns False, the loop never stops. That is an **infinite loop**. It is the classic beginner bug, and every programmer has done it. Forgotten counter, wrong condition. Here the app notices and stops it for you, with a message. Fix the counter or the condition and run again.

watch.intro: Tap Run. It counts three takes, then says wrap.
watch.code:
take = 1
while take <= 3:
    print(f"Take {take}")
    take += 1
print("That's a wrap")
explain: `take` starts at 1. Python asks: is 1 <= 3? Yes, so it runs the pushed-in lines.
`take += 1` makes it 2, and Python jumps back up and asks again. Same for 3.
When take becomes 4 the question is False. The loop ends and the last line runs once.
watch.break_it: Break it on purpose: delete the line `take += 1` and run. The counter never changes, so the question is always True: Take 1, Take 1, Take 1... The app stops it and says a loop is probably running forever. That is the infinite loop. Put the line back.

tasks.title: The loop that never starts
tasks.task: This loop should show `1`, `2`, `3` on separate lines, but it shows nothing. The question is False from the very first check. Change ONE thing so it works.
hints: A while loop only runs if the question is True at the start. Is 1 > 3 True?
You want it to keep going while n is small. Which comparison says that?
Change the second line to: while n <= 3:

tasks.title: Slate takes
tasks.task:
Ask how many takes. Then show `Take 1`, `Take 2` and so on up to that number. Example:

`How many takes? 2`
`Take 1`
`Take 2`
tasks.starter:
total = int(input("How many takes? "))
take = 1
# add your loop here
tasks.solution:
total = int(input("How many takes? "))
take = 1
while take <= total:
    print(f"Take {take}")
    take += 1
hints: Copy the shape from the Watch example. The 3 there becomes total.
while take <= total: then print an f-string, then add 1 to take. All pushed in.

tests.expect:
How many takes? 3
Take 1
Take 2
Take 3

How many takes? 5
Take 1
Take 2
Take 3
Take 4
Take 5

tasks.title: Count the crew
tasks.task:
Keep asking `Crew name (or done)? ` again and again. Stop when the answer is `done`. Count the names you were given and show how many at the end. Example:

`Crew name (or done)? Ana`
`Crew name (or done)? done`
`1 crew`
tasks.starter:
count = 0
# loop here: ask for a name again and again
print(f"{count} crew")
tasks.solution:
count = 0
while True:
    name = input("Crew name (or done)? ")
    if name == "done":
        break
    count += 1
print(f"{count} crew")
hints: Start with while True: so it keeps asking. Inside, use input() and store the answer.
After asking, check: if name == "done": then break. Otherwise add 1 to count.

tests.expect:
Crew name (or done)? Ana
Crew name (or done)? Sipho
Crew name (or done)? done
2 crew

Crew name (or done)? A
Crew name (or done)? B
Crew name (or done)? C
Crew name (or done)? D
Crew name (or done)? done
4 crew

recap: `while condition:` repeats the pushed-in lines as long as the condition is True.
A counter (`n = 1`, then `n += 1`) makes the loop move forward.
`break` leaves the loop at once. `while True:` plus `break` is a common pattern.
If the condition never turns False you have an infinite loop. Check the counter.

words.meaning: Repeat the lines as long as the question is True.
A number that goes up by one each time round.
Add to the name itself: n += 1 means n = n + 1.
Jump out of the loop right now.
A loop that never stops because its question never turns False.
